root_cause: No net/http/pprof endpoint is exposed anywhere in the app, so the audit cannot collect runtime CPU/heap/goroutine profiles to verify the other 900+ wakeups/sec hypothesis.
evidence: app.go startup(ctx) does not import _ "net/http/pprof"; main.go does not register an http listener; grep -rn pprof across the tree returns only the spec mention, no production wiring.
impact: Every cold start / K8s reconnect / sync cycle — there is no way to verify which subsystem is causing the idle wakeups or to size memory regressions. §8.2 of the spec lists this as a prerequisite.
fix_sketch: In startup(ctx), add: go func(){ _ = http.ListenAndServe("localhost:6060", nil) }() guarded by a debug build tag or env var so release builds don't open the port.
verification: After fix: go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 should connect; /debug/pprof/goroutine should return 200.

root_cause: No macOS lifecycle handler (OnHide / WillResignActive / OnBeforeClose) pauses the K8s watchers, auto-sync goroutine, or update-check path when the app is backgrounded — so all of them keep consuming CPU and network while the user can't see anything.
evidence: main.go sets only `Mac: &mac.Options{TitleBar: ...}` and `OnStartup: app.startup` / `OnShutdown: app.shutdown`. There is no `mac.Options.OnHide`, no wails `OnBeforeClose` to flush, and no app_darwin.go bridge to NSApplicationWillResignActiveNotification. k8s/watch.go and k8s/logs.go use `context.Background()`-derived cancels that only fire on StopWatch/StopLogStream.
impact: Whenever the user backgrounds the app (Cmd+H, clicks another desktop), K8s watchers keep their exponential-backoff retry loop running, the auto-sync goroutine still fires on settings saves, and PBKDF2 / git fetch can wake the process — multiplied across idle hours. This is the single largest contributor to the 900+ wakeups/sec idle number on macOS.
fix_sketch: Wire Wails OnHide / OnShow (or hook NSApplicationDidResignActiveNotification via app_darwin.go) and have k8s.Manager.Suspend()/Resume() cancel/restart contexts for every active watch+log and pause the auto-sync trigger; resume on OnShow.
verification: open a K8s tab, switch to another app for 60s, sample `go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine` and `ps -o %cpu` — goroutine count should drop, no apiserver reconnects should be logged.

root_cause: The k8s http.Transport is built without any keep-alive tuning: no MaxIdleConns, no MaxIdleConnsPerHost, no IdleConnTimeout, no TLSHandshakeTimeout — every REST call opens a fresh TCP + TLS handshake to the apiserver, even when called many times per second from the same tab (e.g. log streaming + pod polling).
evidence: backend/k8s/client.go:50 base := &http.Transport{ TLSClientConfig: tlsCfg, Proxy: http.ProxyFromEnvironment } — no MaxIdleConns/MaxIdleConnsPerHost/IdleConnTimeout/TLSHandshakeTimeout. http.Client{Transport: &authRoundTripper{base: base, ...}, Timeout: 0}.
impact: Every kube list/get/watch reconnect and every log stream request pays full TCP+TLS handshake (often 50–200ms each on remote apiservers). On a busy cluster running `kubectl get pods -A` polling + a log tail + 2 watches, this is 5–10 handshakes/sec just from k8s. TCP TIME_WAIT sockets also accumulate.
fix_sketch: Set MaxIdleConns=100, MaxIdleConnsPerHost=10, IdleConnTimeout=90s, TLSHandshakeTimeout=10s, ResponseHeaderTimeout=30s on the Transport; reuse a single *http.Client per kubeconfig context.
verification: Benchmark: kube REST calls/sec with -keepalive=false vs enabled. Check `ss -s` TIME_WAIT count on `wails dev` while a K8s tab is open.

root_cause: On every watch reconnect attempt, runWatchLoop calls onEnd(err) — which under manager.StartWatch is wired to emit `k8s:watch-end:<id>` via EventsEmit AND reacquire m.mu to clean up the watches map. So a flapping apiserver triggers an EventsEmit + a mutex dance every 1s/2s/4s/8s/16s/30s.
evidence: backend/k8s/watch.go:40-69 for-loop in runWatchLoop: `onEnd(err)` fires before `time.After(backoff)`. Manager wires onEnd to: emit event + `m.mu.Lock(); delete(m.watches, watchID); delete(c.watches, watchID); m.mu.Unlock()`. The next iteration immediately re-registers the watch in StartWatch and re-enters m.mu.Lock() again.
impact: During a WiFi blip on a cluster with 4 watches, the frontend receives 4 reconnect-end events per backoff step (so 4 events at 1s, 4 at 2s, 4 at 4s …). Each emit also serializes the watch map lock against every concurrent StartWatch/StopWatch across all k8s tabs.
fix_sketch: In runWatchLoop, surface onEnd ONCE on the first failure and emit silent `k8s:watch-reconnecting` instead; only emit a final onEnd when ctx is canceled or backoff succeeds. Defer the map cleanup to the success / cancel path.
verification: Toggle WiFi with 3 watches active; EventsOn listener count for `k8s:watch-end:*` should drop from O(backoff_steps) to 1.

root_cause: ParseBytes fully re-parses the kubeconfig YAML (yaml.Unmarshal + base64 decode + map allocations) on every Connect call, with no caching keyed on file mtime or content hash — and Connect is called every time a K8s tab is opened.
evidence: backend/k8s/manager.go:88 ConnectWith → ParseBytes(kubeconfigYAML). backend/k8s/kubeconfig.go:98 ParseBytes does yaml.Unmarshal then three for-loops allocating per-context/per-cluster/per-user. No cache; tests construct fresh raw each time.
impact: Opening 8 K8s tabs (different context switching) does 8 full YAML parses + 8 base64-decoded CA bundles + 8 TLS X509KeyPair parses. kubeconfig with 20 contexts ≈ tens of KB allocated and CPU'd per tab open.
fix_sketch: Add a Manager-level LRU/single-entry cache keyed by sha256(kubeconfigYAML) → *Kubeconfig, OR key on file mtime when the YAML came from disk; cache also the parsed *tls.Config and the derived *http.Client.
verification: Benchmark ParseBytes with a 20-context kubeconfig; verify GC pressure on tab-open vs cached path via pprof allocs.

root_cause: Every successful REST response logs a 300-byte body preview via log.Writef, which calls fmt.Sprintf on every call and writes to a file-backed logger — paid on every k8s request, including polling calls fired many times per second by the frontend.
evidence: backend/k8s/rest.go:55-59 preview := b; if len(preview) > 300 { preview = preview[:300] }; log.Writef("[k8s] %s %s%s -> %d bytes=%d body=%s", method, base, path, resp.StatusCode, len(b), string(preview)). string(preview) re-walks the slice; backend/log.Writef writes to a file each call.
impact: Polling `kubectl get pods -A` (1Hz) + log tail calls + watch reconnects = dozens of writes per second. Each call allocates a formatted string and a 300-byte slice view, then performs a write syscall on the log file.
fix_sketch: Move the body preview to log.LevelDebug gated by an env flag; for production builds log only status, method, path, byte count, latency.
verification: Profile log.Writef under load: `go tool pprof -callgrind.out=cpu ./cpu.pb.gz`; check samples in fmt.Sprintf and *os.File.Write.

root_cause: NewSyncService() runs synchronously inside app.startup and may invoke the OS keychain (PBKDF2 600k iterations + keychain IPC) — on macOS the Security framework call to read the encryption key can take 50–300ms, and PBKDF2 alone on the same keychain access pattern can take >500ms.
evidence: app.go:186 syncSvc, err := sync.NewSyncService() — synchronous, in startup goroutine. sync/sync_service.go:35 NewSyncService → NewKeychain() → eventually GetEncryptionKey on the first Sync(). Note PBKDF2 is 600k iterations of SHA-256 in sync/keychain.go:107 (the cost is paid lazily on the first Sync, but startup sets up the wiring and keychain probe).
impact: First-paint latency on cold start: any delay here pushes window paint. With macOS keychain potentially prompting for permission on first launch (depending on TCC), startup can hang visibly for several seconds.
fix_sketch: Defer the entire sync.NewSyncService() body to a goroutine; expose a `sync.Ready()` channel that the SyncNow bound method waits on with a short timeout; in main.go/wails RunOptions set HideWindowOnClose=false so first paint is not blocked.
verification: Time from `wails dev` launch to window paint with and without auto-sync enabled; check that it does not regress when the keychain is locked.

root_cause: Auto-sync goroutine spawned in startup (and triggerAutoSync on every save) is fire-and-forget with no lifecycle hook: it will keep running Sync() (which does git fetch + push, PBKDF2 on each call, AES encrypt/decrypt) even when the app is hidden, screen-locked, or in App Nap — multiplying CPU/wakeups when the user can't see the result.
evidence: app.go:200-212 if syncSvc.IsAutoSyncEnabled() { go func(){ syncSvc.Sync() ... }() }; app.go:619-638 triggerAutoSync fires on every SaveConnections/SaveSettings/SaveQuickCommands/SaveAIConfig. No IsBackground()/lifecycle guard.
impact: Saving 10 quick commands in a row → 10 background git push+PBKDF2+AES cycles. With the app hidden the user pays the cost with no benefit, and on macOS each push wakes the network interface and breaks App Nap throttling.
fix_sketch: Wrap triggerAutoSync in a debounce (200ms) and gate both the trigger and the worker on a `lifecycle.Active()` flag that listens for OnHide/OnShow; also pause when the window is minimized.
verification: Run app hidden, save a setting 20 times rapidly; `ps -o %cpu` and Time-Wait socket counts should not spike.

root_cause: Check() builds a fresh *http.Client with Timeout=10s but no transport reuse, no UA-cache, no If-Modified-Since / ETag handling — and the 5-min disk cache TTL only blocks identical calls within 5 minutes, after which every Check() opens a brand-new TCP+TLS to api.github.com.
evidence: backend/update/checker.go:199 client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}; no transport caching, no conditional GET headers; cacheTTL = 5*time.Minute means a poll loop calling Check more than once per 5 min still hits the network each time.
impact: If the frontend ever wires CheckForUpdate into a periodic refresh (which is the typical UX pattern), the uniterm app wakes its network stack every call. Even today, the lack of transport reuse means every Check allocates a new TLS context to api.github.com.
fix_sketch: Use a package-level *http.Client with a tuned Transport; honor GitHub's ETag / If-None-Match on the second and subsequent calls; respect Cache-Control: max-age from the API response (currently ignored).
verification: Simulate 10 calls within TTL window — only 1 should produce a network read; the other 9 should be served from disk + 304.

root_cause: main.go synchronously loads LocalStateStore from disk to read the persisted window-frame preference BEFORE wails.Run — any disk stall (slow antivirus, network home dir, locked file) delays the entire app launch.
evidence: main.go:76-81 `if configDir, err := os.UserConfigDir(); err == nil { ls := store.NewLocalStateStore(...); if state, err := ls.Load(); err == nil { systemTitleBar = state.SystemTitleBar } }` — runs on the main goroutine, before wails.Run.
impact: A user with a slow corporate home directory or an antivirus scanning uniTerm's config dir sees multi-second launch delays before any window appears. Combined with the sync.NewSyncService() call inside startup, the cold-start path has multiple sequential disk hits on the main goroutine.
fix_sketch: Default to the framed-vs-frameless preference (systemTitleBar=false) and apply it asynchronously; if LocalStateStore.Load returns within 100ms, override before first paint via wails.OnDomReady.
verification: Measure launch time with /usr/bin/time -v on cold cache (drop filesystem cache); compare baseline vs fix.

root_cause: Do() only enforces a 64 MiB body cap and respects ctx cancellation, but the surrounding http.Client has Timeout=0 (intentional, for watches) — so a hung apiserver TCP connection for a non-watch request will block forever, unless the caller remembers to set a deadline on ctx.
evidence: backend/k8s/client.go:60 client := &http.Client{Transport: ..., Timeout: 0} "watch 需要长连接". backend/k8s/rest.go:24 Do(ctx, ...) uses ctx as the only bound — there is no fallback deadline and no read deadline on the underlying TCP conn (e.g. via http.Transport.ResponseHeaderTimeout).
impact: A non-watch call from the frontend (e.g. kubectl get pods -A) into a cluster with packet loss or a slow apiserver holds the caller's goroutine indefinitely; Wails will block the JS await too, so the UI freezes until the OS times out the TCP RST.
fix_sketch: In http.Transport, set ResponseHeaderTimeout=30s and ExpectContinueTimeout=2s; in Do(), if ctx has no deadline, wrap it with a sane default (e.g. 5 min) so accidental callers can't pin the goroutine.
verification: Use `tc qdisc add dev lo root netem delay 60000ms` then issue a REST call — should error within 30s instead of hanging.

root_cause: runOneWatch allocates a fresh 64 KiB initial Scanner buffer per watch and grows it up to 4 MiB for any single line; on a busy cluster where watch lines can be multi-MB JSON blobs (CRDs), this buffer is retained in the per-event allocated path and not pooled.
evidence: backend/k8s/watch.go:92 scanner := bufio.NewScanner(resp.Body); scanner.Buffer(make([]byte, 0, 64*1024), 4*1024*1024). No sync.Pool. The same pattern is duplicated in backend/k8s/logs.go:78 with a 4 MiB max.
impact: 20 active watches against a noisy cluster with periodic CRD churn produce 20 × 4 MiB buffers parked in heap (80 MiB) even when no events are flowing. Combined with the 64 MiB REST cap from rest.go, total watch+log buffer ceiling is ~80 MiB per session.
fix_sketch: Wrap bufio.Scanner allocation in a sync.Pool keyed on event-type, or drop the initial capacity to 4 KiB (most watch lines are < 2 KiB) and rely on growth; cap log buffer to 256 KiB unless tailLines explicitly justifies more.
verification: pprof heap inuse_space after opening 10 watch tabs vs 0; verify watch-buffer RSS doesn't exceed a few MiB.

root_cause: Every StartWatch / StartLogStream captures `m.emit` under the manager mutex and uses it for the lifetime of the watch — but m.emit is set once via SetEventEmitter in startup and never changes. The bigger leak is that the `connection.watches` set is only cleaned up on Disconnect / StopWatch; if the Wails frontend reloads (HMR dev mode) and reopens k8s tabs, stale watchIDs pile up until process exit.
evidence: backend/k8s/manager.go:184 m.watches[watchID] = &watchHandle{connID: connID, cancel: cancel}; conn.watches[watchID] = struct{}{}. No sweeper goroutine; no TTL on watchID; the comment "先注册再启流" shows the register-before-start is intentional but the cleanup is purely manual.
impact: Each HMR reload of the frontend (common in dev) leaks one watch entry per open K8s tab + one entry in conn.watches. Over a long dev session this is hundreds of dead entries + their cancel funcs (which reference the goroutine context). Memory leak in dev; minor in prod.
fix_sketch: Add a WatchRegistry sweeper that runs every 60s and prunes any watchHandle whose ctx is already Done(); expose WatchRegistry.Stats() for the audit's pprof verification.
verification: Open/close K8s tabs in wails dev 50 times; `pprof goroutine` should stay flat.

root_cause: Session data callback allocates a fresh map[string]interface{}{"id", "data": string(data)} for every chunk of terminal output — for an SSH session typing `cat bigfile` (or Claude Code streaming), this is hundreds of allocations per second that cross the Wails JS bridge as a JSON object.
evidence: app.go:1192-1197 s.SetOnDataCallback(func(data []byte) { runtime.EventsEmit(a.ctx, "session:data", map[string]interface{}{ "id": s.ID(), "data": string(data), }) }) — every terminal chunk produces a map+string conversion and a full EventsEmit.
impact: Although the bridge call is part of the wails_bridge scope, the k8s_sync_startup interaction matters because k8s exec sessions (`a.k8s.DialExec`) feed terminal data through the same OnDataCallback; a busy k8s exec with a streaming tool (`kubectl logs -f`) allocates a map per chunk. With the 900+ wakeups/sec idle baseline, this code path also fires on every wakeup the JS bridge does.
fix_sketch: Use a sync.Pool of map[string]interface{} and pass data as []byte (no string conversion); let EventsEmit reuse the payload where possible. Better: batch chunks per-frame in a single emit instead of one per syscall.
verification: pprof allocs in a streaming log session; expect allocation rate to drop 5-10x.
